newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen rebels call elections for January.
newsitem.headline: Chechen rebels call elections for January.

text.p: Chechen separatists, worried about the fate of the latest peace deal with Russia after the sacking of its Moscow author, Alexander Lebed, confirmed plans on Friday to hold elections on January 27.

President Boris Yeltsin's spokesman said Lebed, dismissed from two top security posts on Thursday, would soon be formally sacked as Moscow's envoy to Chechnya. Other top officials said Lebed's departure would not affect the Chechnya peace process.

Itar-Tass news agency said Chechnya's pro-separatist parliament had decided to hold elections for a local legislature and regional leader, confirming an earlier decision by the separatist leadership. It did not say when the decision had been confirmed.

Elections are an eventual goal under the peace deal Lebed signed with the rebels on August 31. They are supposed to be arranged by a joint commission of officials from Moscow and Chechnya but the rebels are pushing ahead without consultation.
Yeltsin sacked Lebed as his national security adviser and secretary of his policy-making Security Council, saying he was sick and tired of his squabbling with other Kremlin officials.
"Lebed's dismissal as the presidential envoy to Chechnya is a matter of time," Yeltsin's spokesman, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, said by telephone. "New candidates for the job are being discussed now."

Lebed told a news conference after his sacking that he would not miss the Kremlin posts but that he regretted losing the post as Yeltsin's envoy in Chechnya and head of Moscow's delegation at peace talks with the Chechen rebels.
Under the August 31 agreement, fighting stopped in Chechnya and Russian troops started leaving the region after 21 months of a campaign in which they suffered some humiliating defeats.

The deal, which also postponed for five years the settlement of a dispute over Chechnya's status, was hailed by ordinary Russians. But many Moscow politicians called it a capitulation which would encourage separatism elsewhere in Russia.

Rebel leaders said on Thursday they saw Lebed's sacking as a sign that the "party of war" was gaining the upper hand in the Kremlin and that they were ready for the resumption of fighting if Moscow broke the terms of the peace deal.
"Everyone is watching the development of events in Moscow with concern," Interfax quoted a senior rebel as saying.
"The leaders of Ichkeria (Chechnya) think that with the dismissal of Lebed, the key factor in the process of a peaceful settlement in Chechnya has been removed."
Lebed's sacking as the main Chechnya negotiator may paradoxically upset his opponents in Moscow.

Many of them want Lebed, who made political gains by ending the fighting, to stay in the job in the hope that his image will be dented during the difficult negotiations that lie ahead on the terms for maintaining the peace.
The rebel leaders made clear they saw the deal as a time-out for Moscow to find a face-saving way to let Chechnya go. Russian officials have ruled out granting independence to Chechnya.

Tass quoted separatist Chechen government representative Akhyad Idigov as saying international observers would be asked to monitor the election, which would choose a president and a parliament for the region.
Representatives of the "opposition" -- the Moscow-backed Chechen government of Doku Zavgayev -- would be invited to join the central electoral commission.
It was not clear if Moscow would recognise the results if the elections went ahead without due consultation.
